chunks.text: On Thursday at 02:50, Lin Yu-Ting started a routine rollout. She is 24 and works on the cloud operations team of a software company in Taipei.
The new routing rule had been tested in the staging environment, and two engineers had signed it off.
It was pushed to the Singapore region first, because that region carries the least traffic at that hour.
At 03:04 the first alert arrived. Requests to one availability zone were timing out.
The dashboard showed healthy servers, which made no sense: the machines were running, but traffic was not reaching them.
Yu-Ting opened the routing table. The new rule sent all traffic to the older zone, where the replica was already under heavy load.
The replica was not down. It was saturated: still running, but unable to answer fast enough.
Latency climbed for four minutes before anyone noticed.
At 03:11 she rolled the change back. Normal traffic returned at 03:19.
The status page was updated once, and it was three sentences long: “A routing change was rolled back. Service was restored at 03:19.
The downtime was fifteen minutes: customers in the affected zone saw an error page, and everyone else noticed nothing.
On Friday morning the team held a post-mortem. Nobody was blamed.
The question was why the staging test had passed. The answer was simple: it had been run against one region, and the problem only appeared when two regions were compared.
Yu-Ting wrote the report in the passive on purpose. “When something breaks at three in the morning,” she says, “the last thing users need is a name.
They need to know what happened, when it will be fixed, and whether their data is safe.”
